Trust is the product

By lowob · 4 June 2026 · 5-minute read · Strategy

In fintech, trust is the product and the feature list is secondary. Trust is borrowed from institutions the buyer already trusts, proved in a fixed order, and every claim you make about money is compliance copy.

Trust is transferred, not created

No ad has ever made someone trust a company with their savings. What an ad can do is point at something the buyer already trusts and say "we are attached to that."

That is the whole mechanism. A licence from a regulator they recognise. A custodian bank whose name they know. A payment network logo. An auditor. An accountant who recommends you. A friend with a funded account.

Your positioning job is to decide which trusted thing you are attached to, and put it where the buyer looks first. Part 2 set a single product truth. In fintech the product truth usually has a second half: "and here is who stands behind it."

If you have nothing trusted to attach to yet, that is your positioning problem. Fix it before you spend on reach.

The order the buyer checks

Fintech buyers run the same checks in roughly the same order, whether they are a consumer, a finance lead at a small business, or a treasury team. The order matters because they stop at the first unanswered question.

Question in the buyer's head What answers it Where it must live
Who is behind this? Named founders, backers, licence, regulator Homepage, first screen
Which institution holds the money? Custodian or partner bank, named, with the protection scheme that applies Homepage, onboarding, FAQ
Who else like me uses it? Customers in their segment, numbers you can stand behind Case pages, onboarding
What happens when something goes wrong? Dispute process, support hours, what's covered, what isn't A page you link to, not a line in terms
What are the fees, actually? A full fee table, including the ones you'd rather not show One page, one table
What do I earn or save? Yield, rate, savings claim, compliance-approved After the above

Most fintech sites invert this table. They answer question six on the hero and question two in the footer. The buyer reads that as a signal.

The claims register is compliance copy

Part 2 introduced the claims register: the list of things you are allowed to say, with the evidence beside each. In most categories it is a sales tool. In fintech it is a compliance document that sales happens to use.

Yield and return claims, safety and protection language, "better than your bank" comparisons, "guaranteed," "free," "instant": each has rules, and the rules differ by market and by licence type. The register records the approved wording, the required disclaimer, the date it was approved, and who approved it.

Then it becomes the only source. Ads, landing pages, creator briefs, partner decks, support macros, the founder's posts. Nobody writes a new claim about money. They pick one from the register.

This is slower on day one and much faster from day thirty. Nothing gets pulled, re-reviewed, or quietly screenshotted by a competitor's lawyer.

Lead with the custodian, not the yield

The yield is the most tempting thing to lead with. It is also the claim most likely to be regulated, the easiest for a competitor to beat next week, and the one the buyer trusts least when it comes first.

Lead instead with the thing that cannot be beaten next week: the licence, the custodian, the protection scheme, the audit. These change slowly and are hard to copy.

A practical rule: the first screen names who holds the money, and the second names what you earn. If the first screen has to be the yield, the custodian goes in the same sentence.

A belief per audience

Part 2 asked for one product truth and one belief per audience. Fintech audiences differ more than most, because they are trusting you with different things.

Consumers need to believe the money is safe and reachable. Their trusted sources are the protection scheme, the bank name, and people they know.

Small businesses need to believe it works with how they already run money: their accountant, their payroll, their bookkeeping software. Their trusted source is the practitioner who already advises them.

Institutions need to believe you will still exist and still be compliant in three years. Their trusted sources are the licence, the audit, the controls, and your reporting.

Investors need to believe trust is converting into funded accounts that stay. A later part of this series covers that evidence.

Four audiences, four beliefs, one product truth, one register. The copy changes. The claims do not.

The checklist

The homepage names who holds the money on the first screen.

A fee page exists with every fee in one table.

A "what happens when something goes wrong" page exists and is linked from onboarding.

The claims register holds approved wording, disclaimer, approval date and approver for every money claim.

Every channel, including creators and partners, pulls copy only from the register.

Each of the four audiences has one written belief and the trusted source that transfers it.

lowob takeaways

  • Trust is transferred from a recognised regulator, custodian bank, payment network, auditor or recommender, not created by ads.
  • Most fintech sites invert the order, putting yield on the hero and the custodian in the footer.
  • The first screen should name who holds the money; the second names what you earn.
